name: Daai Chin
confidence_why: 2 independent first-hand descriptions agree (1 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.

tone_statements.citation: Hartmann, Helga. 2002. Verb stem alternation in Daai Chin. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 25(2): 81-97. doi:10.32655/ltba.25.2.05. Open PDF:http://sealang.net/sala/archives/pdf8/hartmann2002verb.pdf(also NTU LTBA archive hdl 10356/178016)
tone_statements.quote: Therefore in this paper high tone is marked with a colon following the vowel, and mid-level tone is unmarked. But Daai Chin has more than one high tone. There are at least high falling and high tense (creaky) tones to be distinguished. ... But there are cases when high tense tone and high falling tone do not occur in complementary distribution. The orthography used in this paper does not show this differentiation. Also, apart from mid level tone (unmarked) and the two high tones, there is a low falling tone unmarked in the orthography and in this paper.
tone_statements.summary: Preliminary fn. inventory: mid-level, high falling, high tense (creaky), low falling ('at least'; analysis deferred; varies by village). Only high (V:) vs mid marked; Class IV(b,c) stem B always high.

tone_statements.quote: Tone: Plain level tone vs. tense high falling tone. The high tense tone does not occur on short syllables with a final stop. ... 2. Rule II. Loss of high tense tone 2.1 Unconditional loss of high tense tone ... If the first member of a compound noun is an open syllable with high tense tone and is followed by simple consonant or preglottalization it always changes into a plain tone.
tone_statements.locator: p.180 sec. 2.3 'Vowel modifications: Tone'; p.183 sec. B.2 Rule IIa
tone_statements.summary: Two-way contrast: plain level vs tense high falling (marked with acute); high tense tone barred on short stop-final syllables and lost on first members of compounds (Rules IIa-IIe). No word on stress.

audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant, rule 01: unstressed presyllable + stressed main syllable) rests on the standard 392-pp reference grammar (So-Hartmann 2009), which I downloaded from the STEDT site and in which the deciding quotation appears verbatim at sec. 2.1, printed p. 35; the whole stress treatment (pp. 35-37) is unhedged and matches the classification, and every stress mention in the book is in that section. Two further open sources downloaded now agree: Hartmann 2001 (LTBA 24.2, p.124) states the syllabic-nasal and glottal presyllables are unstressed; Mortensen 2023 (Himalayan Linguistics) restates the Daai sesquisyllabic minor+major structure without a stress claim; Hartmann-So 1989 is silent on stress. No copies we hold existed before this compilation; the source is now Housekeeping only: repair the truncated cite string ('via extracted text

sources.quote: That is, the PW is always constituted of a stressed syllable 'S, which may optionally be preceded by an unstressed syllabic constituent (S). I will refer to the preposed unstressed element as a PRESYLLABLE and the stressed one as the MAIN SYLLABLE.

sources.citation: So-Hartmann, Helga. 2009. A Descriptive Grammar of Daai Chin. STEDT Monograph Series 7. Berkeley: Sino-Tibetan Etymological Dictionary and Thesaurus Project, University of California. 392 pp. (open PDF from stedt.johnblowe.com/pubs_and_prods/)
sources.quote: 'the PW is always constituted of a stressed syllable 'S, which may optionally be preceded by an unstressed syllabic constituent (S)' (p.35); 'These two-syllabic phonological words involve a weakly stressed syllable (WS) closely-knit with a following strongly stressed dominant or main syllable (SS)... metrically iambic contours' (p.35); 'no other phonological material may be inserted between the Presyllable and the Mainsyllable, that is, the sequence constitutes a cohesive stress contour' (p.36); presyllable inventory reduced to syllabic m-, n-, ng-, glottal, and vowel a- (p.37).

tone.says: As the thesis version of the 2009 monograph it should contain the same sec. 2.4 'Tone': two contrastive lexical tones, a mid-level tone called 'low' (unmarked) and a high-falling tone called 'high'; no tone contrast in closed syllables with short vowels and stop codas, contrast in all other syllable types (open, long vowel, nasal/semivowel codas), with minimal pairs; discussion rejecting a tonal analysis of the final glottal stop; tone as an exponent of verb stem A/B alternation; orthography ab…

sources.quote: Describes Daai (after So-Hartmann 2009: 38) as sesquisyllabic with minor syllables that 'often consist of a single consonant without a vocalic nucleus' preceding full major syllables; no explicit statement of stress placement.
